title: Silas and the Vanishing Feather
markdown:
Once upon a time Silas the deer lived in a village tucked beside a whispering forest, hooves as quick with pruning shears as with trowels. His greenhouse was a riot of green, a marvel of prize orchids. Every day he tended plants, and every day he also yearned to capture fleeting moments—a passion the town, which prized practical crafts, found wildly unfashionable. Photography magazines slid from high shelves when his antlers nudged them.

Until one day a crisp notice, carried by a wind that rattled the glass, announced the annual Village Portrait Competition. The grand prize made his ears twitch. Not a stern elder, not a prize pig: stacked antique books, worn spines whispering, and a tiny iridescent feather perched on the tallest volume, a feather that would make the portrait sing of forgotten dreams.

Because of that he turned a corner into a studio. A deep crimson velvet curtain, ripped from an old theatre prop, became the backdrop. Leather bindings smelled of dust. He fussed with lamps for a subtle light. Then the feather, the heart of the vision, vanished. Antlers drooped toward potting soil.

Rowan the crow, assistant, squawk loud as his wings were black, flitted and declared, “Maybe it flew off for more shiny things. I’ll check the compost heap.” Rowan meant well. His idea of art was anything that glittered, a stark contrast to Silas’s subtle hopes.

Because of that a frantic search: cawing chaos, deer desperation. Rowan scattered polished river stones, convinced the feather hid among them. Silas peered into watering cans and soil bags. He sifted pruned rose bushes, thorns mirroring panic. The deadline loomed like a thundercloud. He slumped against the workbench. “No use. Petunias are more my speed.”

Rowan paused pebble-sorting. “Nonsense. Your ideas are… interesting.” High praise.

Until finally a tiny chirp. Pipkin the wren, no bigger than a teacup, usually only spoke of sunrise or worms, sat almost invisible on a high shelf and nudged the iridescent feather, snagged on a cobweb. Hope surged like a spring shower. Silas scrambled, hooves tapping floorboards, velvet rustling, damp soil rising from overturned pots. He snatched the feather as last moonlight slanted through the panes and bathed the books. A steady breath. He captured the image.

Ever since then the portrait—moonlight on stacked books—won first prize. The village, initially perplexed, grew to admire the unfashionable idea. The greenhouse thrived with plants and a quieter hum of making. Rowan still loved shiny things. He had also learned that some treasures do not glitter. Silas, who had begun among orchids and unread magazines, left the velvet up and the feather in its place on the tallest spine, no longer a dream in hiding.
